name: Addis Ababa
info: Addis Ababa is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia, standing high in the Ethiopian Highlands at the foot of Mount Entoto. It was founded in 1886 by Empress Taytu Betul and Menelik II and became the imperial capital in 1889.

facts.founded: Settlement began in 1886 at Finfinne, a place of hot springs; the site was chosen by Empress Taytu Betul, and Menelik II, Negus of Shewa, moved his court there. The city became the capital of the empire in 1889.
facts.where: In the Ethiopian Highlands at an elevation of 2,355 metres, at the foot of Mount Entoto and on the western edge of the Great Rift Valley, in Ethiopia and surrounded by the Special Zone of Oromia.
facts.known: Taytu's house by the hot springs; Menelik II's capital; the Italian occupation of 1936 to 1941; Haile Selassie's return in 1941; the headquarters of the Organisation of African Unity and the African Union; the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa; the Merkato market
facts.today: Addis Ababa is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia, a federally chartered city with an estimated 6.3 million inhabitants.

t: Addis Ababa began in 1886 as a royal camp beside hot springs, laid out like an army on the march, and became the capital of Menelik II's empire in 1889.

Italian troops entered the city on 5 May 1936 and held it until 1941, when Haile Selassie returned on the fifth anniversary of his departure; later plans by Italian, British and French consultants shaped its growth.
Haile Selassie was deposed in 1974 by the Derg, the EPRDF seized the city in 1991, and the capital became the seat of the Organisation of African Unity and its successor, the African Union.

sections.origins:
Addis Ababa stands in the Ethiopian Highlands at an elevation of 2,355 metres, at the foot of Mount Entoto, on the western edge of the Great Rift Valley. A DNA study of almost 1,000 people has suggested that early humans left Africa by a route close to the city some 100,000 years ago. Mount Entoto is one of a few sites proposed as the location of Barara, a fortified imperial capital of the 15th and early 16th centuries that was razed and plundered by Ahmad ibn Ibrahim in 1529. A large medieval town found between the rock-hewn Washa Mikael and the church of Entoto Maryam, covering 30 hectares and including a castle with 12 towers, has been cited in support of that proposal. In the centuries before the city's foundation the Gafat people lived in the area. From the late 16th century Oromo groups moving north drove many of them across the Abbay river into Gojjam and absorbed those who remained.

In 1881 Menelik, then Negus of Shewa, moved his capital from Ankober to Entoto. In 1886 settlement began in the valley south of the mountain, in a place called Finfinne, a name that refers to its hot springs. Empress Taytu Betul chose the site and built a house near the springs, where she and members of the Shewan court liked to take mineral baths. She persuaded Menelik II to move down from cold and windy Entoto and named the new city Addis Ababa, 'new flower'. The local Oromo lost their lands, and many were displaced.
sections.growth:
By the next year, 1887, large plots had been allocated to the major nobility, other important people and some churches, and in 1889 Menelik expanded his wife's house into the Imperial Palace. Addis Ababa became the capital of the empire in 1889, and embassies were opened soon afterwards. In 1891 Menelik ordered French engineers to build the first stone houses. Growth was rapid after the Battle of Adwa, which brought some of Ethiopia's first modern roads and large estates for notables who had served in the battle. By 1910 the city had about 70,000 permanent inhabitants and between 30,000 and 50,000 temporary ones.

The railway to Djibouti, linked to the city in 1916, and the rise of Ras Tafari, later Haile Selassie, after 1917 were followed by an economic boom in 1926 and 1927, driven by a surplus of coffee. The middle class built stone houses with imported European furniture and expanded the banks, and registered automobiles rose from 76 in 1926 to 578 in 1930. Before the Italian invasion the population was estimated at between 100,000 and 200,000, including 6,000 foreigners.

After 1941 consultants drew up successive master plans: Sir Patrick Abercrombie's from 1946, an improved version by Bolton Hennessy and Partners in 1959 and a French plan in 1965, when the city covered 21,000 hectares.
sections.rulers:
Addis Ababa was founded by Menelik II, who was Negus of Shewa and later emperor, and by his wife Taytu Betul. It was the capital of the Ethiopian Empire from 1889. Ras Tafari Mekonnen, later Emperor Haile Selassie, was the most powerful figure in the city after his appointment in 1917, gained power as regent in 1918 and was crowned in 1930. He installed power lines and telephones and erected monuments, among them one to Menelik II.

Italian troops entered the city on 5 May 1936 after the major engagements of their invasion. Addis Ababa was then the capital of Italian East Africa under the Duke of Aosta until 1941, when the Italians left it for Amba Alagi and other redoubts during the East African Campaign. Haile Selassie returned on 5 May 1941, five years to the day after he had left, and began re-establishing his capital.

Haile Selassie remained in power until 1974, when a group of police officers deposed him; the group named itself the Derg, officially the Provisional Military Administrative Council. On 28 May 1991 the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front, a coalition overthrowing the Derg, seized the city. Under the constitution of 1995 Addis Ababa is a federal city, chartered by Proclamation No. 87/1997, and it does not have the status of a state.
sections.life:
The city began as a katama, a royal camp. Its sefer, the large plots of the nobles, were laid out as an army is drawn up on the march: the Imperial Palace stood in the centre, flanked by the leaders of the left and right wings, with the lands of Fitawrari Habte Giyorgis furthest to the west. Each sefer was settled by its noble's retainers and slaves, usually brought from the lands he controlled. The Amhara, Oromo, Gurage, Dorze and Tigrayans came in the largest numbers. Artisans, merchants and foreign visitors also arrived, among them Europeans, Armenians and Indians, and the British, French, Italians and Russians later opened legations. Early houses were circular huts with walls of mud and straw plastered on a wooden frame and thatched roofs. Menelik had many eucalyptus trees planted along the streets.

In 1906 Menelik opened the first public school in the city, a break with an education long dominated by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church. The emperor's own press, the Berhanena Salam Printing Press, opened in December 1929. Addis Ababa University was founded in 1950 as the University College of Addis Ababa and was renamed in 1962 for Haile Selassie.

The census of 2007 counted 2,739,551 inhabitants. The largest groups were the Amhara at 47.05 per cent and the Oromo at 19.51 per cent, and 43 per cent of the people were Ethiopian Orthodox and 33 per cent Muslim.
sections.crises:
According to Richard Pankhurst, the city's early growth owed something to the famine of 1892, as well as to provincial governors and their troops and to the Battle of Adwa. The Italian invasion followed in 1935 and 1936. Italian troops entered Addis Ababa on 5 May 1936, and the city was held until 1941. On 19 February 1937 two Eritrean men, Abraha Deboch and Mogus Asgedom, threw grenades at an alms distribution and wounded the viceroy, Marshal Rodolfo Graziani. The Federal Secretary, Guido Cortese, gave his men three days to kill and destroy, and Italians killed Ethiopians with daggers and truncheons and burned houses. Estimates of the dead range from 1,400 to 6,000 in French and American newspapers, and 3,000 for Angelo Del Boca and Anthony Mockler, to 19,200 in a 2017 study by Ian L. Campbell and 30,000 in Ethiopian sources. St George's Cathedral, named for the ark carried at the Battle of Adwa, was ruined by the Fascist Italian government in 1937 and rebuilt after the liberation in 1941.

The 1973 oil crisis heavily affected the city, and 1,500 peasants in Addis Ababa marched to plead for food. Intellectuals from Addis Ababa University pressed the government to act on the spreading famine, and Haile Selassie's government denounced their report as a fabrication. Students gathered to protest in February 1974, and Haile Selassie was deposed that year.

In 1975 the Derg nationalised extra rental buildings, and about two thirds of the housing stock had passed to rental housing. In April 2014 a plan to expand the city's boundaries by 1.1 million hectares into the Special Zone of Oromia set off the Oromo protests. The government responded by shooting at and beating protesters, and about 140 had been killed by the time the plan was cancelled on 12 January 2016.
sections.legacy:
Haile Selassie helped form the Organisation of African Unity in 1963 and invited it to keep its headquarters in Addis Ababa. It was dissolved in 2002 and replaced by the African Union, which is also headquartered in the city, as is the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa, founded in 1958. The city has been called the political capital of Africa. Africa Hall, where the Organisation of African Unity was founded, stands across Menelik II Avenue from the National Palace.

Menelik's old Imperial Palace remains the official seat of government. Holy Trinity Cathedral, the headquarters of the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church, holds the tombs of Haile Selassie, his wife Menen Asfaw and Sylvia Pankhurst. St George's Cathedral was founded in 1896. The Piazza district shows the Italian influence of the occupation, and the Merkato is the largest open market in Africa. The National Museum of Ethiopia keeps the fossil skeleton of the early hominid known as Lucy, or Dinkinesh.

Addis Ababa is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia, with an estimated 6.3 million inhabitants, and its status as a chartered city and its relation to the surrounding Oromia region remain matters of dispute.

summary: Addis Ababa was founded in 1886 by Empress Taytu Betul and Menelik II beside the hot springs of Finfinne and became the imperial capital in 1889. It was the capital of Italian East Africa from 1936 to 1941 and is the seat of the African Union.
references: Richard Pankhurst, The Ethiopians: A History (Wiley-Blackwell, 2001)
notes: REVISED: the massacre of 19 to 21 February 1937 (Yekatit 12) added to 'crises' from the article 'Yekatit 12', and a 1937 key event added. To keep 8 events the 1881 event (Menelik's move to Entoto, also told in 'origins') was dropped.

MASSACRE FIGURES: the article gives 30,000 (Ethiopian sources), 1,400 to 6,000 (French and American newspapers; its lead says 'typically'), 3,000 (Del Boca and Mockler), 19,200 (Campbell, 2017, said to be 20 per cent of the city's population). All given. The article also says 'between 1,400 and 30,000'. Duration: three days (from the afternoon of Friday 19 February). Cortese's order: 'carte blanche' for three days. Executions, camps and the Debre Libanos killings of May are not told here.

DISAGREEMENT: the history article says the war brought heavy aerial bombardment of the city; the main article says Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa were spared aerial bombardment and chemical weapons. Left out. The sentence on 15,000 chemical-weapon victims (Soviet estimates, for Ethiopia, not the city) was cut from 'crises' to keep the section within 1,900 characters.

DISAGREEMENT: the main article says the city was liberated on 5 May 1941 by Orde Wingate; the history article says British forces with the Arbegnoch. Only Haile Selassie's return on 5 May 1941 is stated.
DISAGREEMENT: the history article says the Imperial Palace 'remains the seat of government'; the main article says it is the official seat of government. Used the second.

Founding date 1886 as both give it; the history article puts Taytu's house in 1886 to 1887 and the settlement's naming in 1887. Capital 'between 1889 and 1891' in the history article, 1889 in the main article; used 1889.
Woreda and sub-city counts differ between articles and were left out. The Derg's 1986 plan: 207 (main) or 237 (history) sectorial reports; left out.

Barara: the articles only propose Entoto as one possible site; the 160,000 population estimate for Barara was left out as too speculative. Whether Ahmad ibn Ibrahim's 1529 raid is attributed to Barara is hedged accordingly.
Street/road details (Djibouti road 97 miles or 156 km) left out as the two articles garble the route. Haile Selassie's coronation year 1930 from the main article only.
Population: 2,739,551 in 2007; the estimate of about 6.3 million is the main article's 2025 figure written without the year.

Recent events (2014 protests, Sheger City, Riverside project) kept to the dated protest facts; the criticism of Sheger City and Abiy Ahmed's projects were left out. The 2022 population estimate was left out.

The remark that the Oromo were 'physically removed' from the vicinity under Haile Selassie and the Derg is a claim in the article's Oromia section; not used. Status dispute in the last paragraph is stated in general terms from that section and the 2014 protests.
Barara and Taytu's request to build a house: the anecdote with Menelik's words is told 'is said to have' in the history article; left out.
